rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose possible drug rash / Diagnose possible HIV seroconversion illness / Diagnose probable non-specific viral rash
rule_level_problems.problem: All three depend on the onset of an Exposure finding. The house standard says onset is captured when a finding is recorded, so a long-standing medication (e.g. ART for years) or an old HIV exposure recorded at this visit would get onset = now. Drug rash would then fire for every patient with any recorded medication, seroconversion would fire for any recorded HIV exposure, and non-specific viral rash could only fire on (no exposure). The logic is right only if the onset is entered explicitly.

Because Generalized rash is_a Skin lesion and 'unexplained' cannot be represented, possible mpox fires for almost every generalised-rash patient who has headache, fatigue, cough or any other common symptom, including patients with a reactive syphilis result or a recent drug start. This is broader than the page intends.

rule_level_problems.rule: HIV seroconversion vs non-specific viral rash
rule_level_problems.problem: The boundaries overlap: (<= onset 6 weeks) and (>= onset 6 weeks) are both true at exactly 6 weeks, so possible seroconversion and probable viral rash fire together on that day.

The 'non-itchy' part of the presenting complaint is not encoded, so these rules (e.g. probable non-specific viral rash) also fire for itchy generalised rash, which belongs on a different page. Generalized rash is not a common symptom; the rules fire only if another task records it.

rule_level_problems.rule: Diagnose probable non-specific viral rash (generalised rash page)
rule_level_problems.problem: The rule does not exclude the earlier bullets (tick bite fever, mpox, drug rash), so it can be probable alongside probable tick bite fever in the same patient. The page orders those bullets first, but it does not say explicitly that they exclude viral rash.

'Human immunodeficiency virus detected' is not checked for, so the 'HIV positive' branch result cannot be recorded from this task. This is harmless for the rules because that branch only routes to routine HIV care.

summary: The diagnostic logic is complete and faithful: tick bite fever (probable), mpox (possible), drug rash (possible), secondary syphilis (probable), HIV seroconversion (possible) and non-specific viral rash (probable), with the right thresholds and branch conditions. The most consequential risk is that three rules depend on the onset of an Exposure finding; if onset defaults to the recording time, drug rash and seroconversion over-fire and viral rash under-fires. Minor issues: 'at risk of HIV' is collapsed to a single exposure concept, possible mpox is very broad without 'unexplained', the two rules overlap at exactly 6 weeks, and a closer SNOMED concept exists for generalised drug eruption.
